title: If students are banned from using AI, is it fair for teachers to use it?
author: Daisy Christodoulou
summary: Christodoulou answers the charge of hypocrisy that arises when students are barred from using AI to write assessments while teachers use it to help mark. Her argument rests on a distinction between process and product: for students the assessment sample matters only as evidence of the wider domain of understanding, so outsourcing the work defeats its purpose. For professionals such as accountants, doctors and, she argues, teachers, what matters is the quality of the final product, provided they catch and own the AI's mistakes. She adds a teacher-specific caveat that children care whether a human actually read their work, so AI marking must be designed to retain human input. She closes by describing a model in which two human teachers read every piece, with AI supplementing judgements and turning audio comments into written feedback.
points: The sample-versus-domain principle explains why AI-written student work is worthless as evidence: the assessment only matters for what it reveals about understanding.
For professionals, including teachers, the product matters more than the process, so AI that speeds marking and feedback is positive.
The professional remains accountable for AI outputs, and Christodoulou expects checking and choosing tools to become a growing part of expertise.
Teachers carry an extra obligation because students want their work read by a human, so AI marking should preserve human judgement.
Her proposed model keeps two teachers reading each piece, with AI transcribing audio comments and compiling feedback.
quotes: If all we cared about was the product, then it would be the second student. But we don’t. We care about the process. The first student’s response has led to them learning more and their essay represents greater understanding of the topic than the second student’s essay.

The basic assessment principle here is the difference between the sample and the domain. The sample is the test itself. The domain is the student’s wider understanding. The sample only matters if it tells us something valuable about the domain — otherwise it is worthless. This is one of the most fundamental principles of assessment – and one of the most poorly understood.

Of course, there is a caveat to this. If the AI tool produces a mistake, I expect the professional to catch the mistake, and if they don’t, I am holding them responsible, not the AI tool. I suspect that this might become a growing aspect of a professional’s job.

Broadly speaking, I think teachers are like doctors & accountants in that we care about the product, not the process. If a teacher says they can use an AI tool to speed up the process of marking, return marked work to students quicker, provide more personalised feedback and potentially allow for more work to be set and marked, then that is all positive.

But there is perhaps also a further caveat that only applies to teachers – which is that students often really care about what their teachers think about their work and want their teacher to read what they have written and have an opinion about it.
I don’t really care how much human attention my tax return gets – I just want it to be accurate. A ten year old does really care about whether their teacher has read their work or not.

This model is much quicker & more accurate than the current model, and involves each piece of writing being read by two teachers, not one - which is twice as many as most traditional non-AI approaches to marking.
